stem: A boy with haemophilia is attending a community clinic for vaccination; which approach is best supported?

options.text: Avoid vaccination altogether because any injection is contraindicated
Use the standard intramuscular route without any extra local measures
Consider a subcutaneous route instead of intramuscular, and apply firm pressure for 5-10 minutes
Mix the vaccine with local anaesthetic to reduce bleeding risk
Prime the administration needle before giving the vaccine

explanation: Consider a subcutaneous route instead of intramuscular, and apply firm pressure for 5-10 minutes. This reduces the risk of local bleeding and haematoma in a child with haemophilia.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because vaccination is not contraindicated solely due to haemophilia.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because the notes recommend modifying the route and applying local pressure rather than using standard intramuscular administration without precautions.
optionExplanations.C: Correct because a subcutaneous route can be considered instead of intramuscular injection, and firm pressure for 5-10 minutes helps reduce bleeding and haematoma risk.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because the notes do not recommend mixing the vaccine with local anaesthetic.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because the notes do not recommend priming the administration needle.
